# SK3040 — The `lock` is taken over a synchronization primitive

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `lock` statement is taken over an object that is itself a synchronization primitive — a `SemaphoreSlim`, a `ReaderWriterLockSlim`, or anything below `WaitHandle`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `SuspiciousLockOverSynchronizationPrimitive` (`resharper_suspicious_lock_over_synchronization_primitive_highlighting`) |

## Why

Every reference type carries a monitor, so `lock (semaphore)` compiles. It gives the author a monitor they did not mean, taken over an object whose own waiting happens somewhere else entirely: a thread parked inside `semaphore.Wait()` holds nothing the monitor knows about, and a thread inside `lock (semaphore)` excludes nobody who calls `Wait`. The two mechanisms do not compose, and where the primitive takes its own monitor internally the mistake is a deadlock rather than a no-op. The code above it reads as though the object were guarded, which is the expensive part.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Queue {
    readonly SemaphoreSlim slots = new(4);

    int depth;

    public void Push() {
        lock (slots) {
            depth++;
        }
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Queue {
    readonly SemaphoreSlim slots = new(4);

    int depth;

    public void Push() {
        slots.Wait();
        try {
            depth++;
        } finally {
            slots.Release();
        }
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Fixless, and not for want of trying.** The repair is to decide which mechanism the code meant — take the primitive properly, or introduce a separate lock object — and no edit can choose between those without knowing what the other threads do. Rewriting `lock (semaphore) { … }` into `semaphore.Wait()/Release()` changes which threads are excluded, and introducing a new field changes the type's shape; both are design decisions. ⚠ **This is not `SK1023` and never overlaps it.** `SK1023` looks at a private `readonly object` field whose only use is as a lock target and modernizes a lock that is already correct; this rule never fires on `object`, so the two are disjoint by the lock target's type. ⚠ **`System.Threading.Lock` is excluded explicitly** — it is a synchronization primitive and it is also the one type a C# 13 `lock` statement is supposed to be taken over, since the compiler lowers it to `Lock.EnterScope` rather than to `Monitor`; reporting it would contradict `SK1023`'s own fix. ⚠ The type is resolved from the compilation and never matched on the written name: `Semaphore` and `Barrier` are plausible names for somebody's own type. ⚠ **Stated scope limit:** the rule matches the `lock` statement only. `Monitor.Enter(semaphore)` is the same mistake spelled without the keyword and is not reported, because deciding that the matching `Exit` runs on every path is a different analysis; the negative fixture set records that rather than hiding it. `lock (this)` and `lock (someCollection)` are their own arguments and are not this one.
